summary: An experimental protocol layered on HTTP that lets a server hold several versions of the same resource under one URL, such as different languages or formats, and pick the best one for each client automatically. The aim was to make it easier to roll out new data formats and markup.

plainLanguage.summary: One web address, many versions of the same page. This lets the computer pick the version that suits you best, like a waiter bringing the menu in your language.

questions: how does http choose between variants
what does the alternates header do
what is http status 506 variant also negotiates
subtitle: Let one web address serve several versions of a page, and have the best one picked automatically.

tldr.problem: A site may keep several versions (variants) of a resource under one URI, such as different languages or formats. Sending big Accept headers with every request to choose among them does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: The server returns a compact list of variants and their properties, and the user agent picks the best one and fetches it. Small Accept headers, caches and an optional remote selection algorithm can shorten this to a single round trip.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2295 is Experimental. It adds the Negotiate, Alternates, TCN, Accept-Features and Variant-Vary headers and the 506 status code on top of HTTP/1.x, and defines no remote algorithm itself.

today: RFC 2295 is an Experimental memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It names RFC 2296 as the companion for the remote variant selection algorithm RVSA/1.0, and does not define any remote algorithm itself.

sections.title: One URI, Many Variants
sections.content:
HTTP lets a site author put multiple versions of the same information under a single URI. Each version is a variant. Transparent content negotiation is an extension on top of HTTP/1.1 for automatically and efficiently retrieving the best variant on a GET or HEAD request. It can also be used when some or all parties speak HTTP/1.0.

It is called transparent because it makes every variant that exists inside the origin server visible to outside parties. The stated benefits include smooth deployment of new data formats and markup tags, serving everything from low-end PDAs to high-end VR setups, avoiding error-prone and cache-unfriendly User-Agent based negotiation, multi-lingual content without bias toward one language, and no more click here for the X version links.

The memo notes that related IETF work, such as a protocol-independent feature tag registry, was under way and that it was unclear how far future specifications would reuse this protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: A website can keep the same page in English, French and as a PDF, all behind one address. This paper explains how your browser gets the right one without you clicking around.

sections.title: How the Negotiation Works
sections.content:
The old HTTP/1.0 style has the user agent send Accept headers describing every capability and preference, and the origin server chooses. That does not scale: for all but the most minimal user agents those headers would be very large, and only a small fraction of web resources have variants at all.

In the transparent scheme the server instead sends a list response: a variant list in an Alternates header, plus an HTML body so a person can choose by hand. The user agent chooses and sends a second, completely ordinary request for the variant. Other parties see that second request as normal HTTP.

Two shortcuts cut that round trip. Caching proxies can keep both lists and variants. And the user agent can send small Accept headers so that a server or proxy running a remote variant selection algorithm can answer with a choice response, which carries the chosen variant directly. A server may do this only if the user agent allows a particular algorithm in its Negotiate header, and the chosen variant must be a neighboring variant (same URL up to the last slash).

Four dimensions can be negotiated: media type, charset, language and features. Content encoding is left outside. The memo expects typical variant lists of 2 to 10 variants, and advises against hundreds.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of your browser shouting every wish to the shop, the shop shows a short menu and your browser orders. If the shop already guesses right, it skips the menu and just brings the dish.

sections.title: Variant Descriptions and Feature Negotiation
sections.content:
A variant description looks like {"paper.2" 0.7 {type text/html} {language fr}}. It gives the variant URI, a source quality, and optional attributes: type, charset, language, length, features, description and extensions (experimental ones must start with x-). A variant resource may itself vary, but it must not do transparent negotiation.

Source quality runs from 1.000 (perfect representation) down through 0.900 (threshold of noticeable loss), 0.800, 0.500 and 0.300 to 0.000 (completely degraded). Because quality factors are multiplied together, meaningful values sit close to 1. Servers should not fold file size into this number; size belongs in the length attribute.

The features attribute adds a fourth dimension. A feature tag names something negotiable, such as tables or colordepth. Feature predicates like !textonly, paper=a4 or dpi=[300-599] are tested against the user agent's feature set, and each predicate multiplies the variant's quality by an improvement or degradation factor. This specification defines no feature tags; x. tags are encouraged for experiments.
sections.plainLanguage: Each version on the menu comes with a score for how good it is and little labels like language or format. Extra labels, like needs color screen, let the browser rule out versions that will not work for you.

sections.title: New Status Code and Headers
sections.content:
The memo adds one status code and several headers. The Negotiate request header carries directives: trans (the agent supports transparent negotiation), vlist (always include the variant list), guess-small (let the server guess if the reply stays small), a remote algorithm version number, or an asterisk wildcard (any algorithm).

The TCN response header marks a transparently negotiated response and gives its type: list, choice or adhoc. It may also say re-choose or keep when the server has overridden the normal rules to work around a buggy client. The Alternates response header carries the complete variant list, an optional single fallback variant and a proxy-rvsa directive that limits which algorithms proxies may use. Accept-Features lets a user agent reveal parts of its feature set, and Variant-Vary records vary information that belongs to the variant rather than the whole response.

Status 506 Variant Also Negotiates flags a server configuration error: the chosen variant is itself set up for transparent negotiation, so it is not a valid end point.
sections.plainLanguage: These are new labels on the envelopes. One says what the browser can do, one lists the menu, and one says what kind of answer this is.

sections.title: Responses, Caching and Who Does What
sections.content:
Every 2xx response, and every 3xx response except 304, from a transparently negotiable resource must be a list, choice or adhoc response with a TCN header. A list response carries the Alternates header and a Vary header, and the 300 status code is the most appropriate. A choice response is the chosen variant's normal response plus TCN: choice, a Content-Location header and, as required, the variant list. An adhoc response is an extreme measure for non-negotiating or buggy clients and has few requirements.

For caches, entity tags in negotiated responses must be structured: the normal tag is joined by a semicolon to a variant list validator, as in "etag;vlv". Cacheable negotiated responses must carry a Vary header, either Vary: * or an elaborate one built from negotiate plus the headers matching the attributes in use. An optional past Expires date helps HTTP/1.0 caches.

User agents must be able to turn a list response into a chosen variant, SHOULD reject a choice response for a non-neighboring variant as a probable spoof, and SHOULD let users review all variants and show the negotiable URI rather than the variant URI. Origin servers must always be able to send a list response, and a proxy may reuse a cached Alternates header or extract a normal response from a choice response. Negotiation applies only to GET and HEAD, not to the direct result of a POST.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone along the way must label answers clearly so helpers who keep copies do not hand you the French page when you wanted English.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
Accept headers, especially Accept-Language, can reveal personal information. This scheme lets a user agent omit them by default, but picking a variant still shows a preference. The memo describes a malicious author who offers fake negotiability on languages correlated with ethnicity, with every variant actually the same English page, to harvest that information. A user who reviews the variant list would spot it.

Caching the normal response extracted from a choice response hands the negotiable resource's author control over caches for neighboring variants. This is a problem if a neighboring variant belongs to another author, so servers have to filter Content-Location values. A normal response for a non-neighboring variant must never be cached.

Finally, malicious servers could use negotiation on scripting languages and libraries to learn about security holes in user agents.
sections.plainLanguage: Telling a website your language can tell it things about you. And one author must not be able to trick a shared cache into storing someone else's page.

data.title: Alternates variant list

items.label: List response
items.desc: Returns the variant list but no variant data. Only the origin server may build it.

items.label: Choice response
items.desc: Returns the best neighboring variant, and may also return the list.

items.label: Adhoc response
items.desc: Last resort for non-negotiating or buggy clients, with very few requirements.
